source: OECD (2025), Health at a Glance 2025: OECD Indicators, OECD Publishing, Paris
framing: Gap framing: every figure is what is NOT covered, NOT satisfied or unmet. Gap figures are 100 minus the published figure.
rule: HAL may phrase these facts freely but must not state any figure, ranking or claim that is not in this list. Verbatim report sentences may name other countries; only what they say about this country may be used.

facts.text: 20% of people in Japan were NOT satisfied with the availability of quality healthcare where they live in 2024, versus an OECD average of 36%.
15.2% of health spending in Japan was NOT covered by government or compulsory insurance schemes in 2023, versus an OECD average of 24.9%.
8% of hospital care costs in Japan were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 11% on average in the OECD.
14% of outpatient medical care costs in Japan were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 22% on average in the OECD.
21% of dental care costs in Japan were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 68% on average in the OECD.
29% of pharmaceutical costs in Japan were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 42% on average in the OECD.
In general, doctors were more evenly distributed across regions in Belgium, Japan and Korea.
In Japan, where regional disparities in doctors are small, 16% of all medical students are from a regional quota scholarship programme.
Disparities were smallest in Czechia, France and Japan, where more than 98% of people in rural areas had access to hospitals nearby.
In some countries, doctors are paid predominantly by fee-for-service (as in Germany, Japan, Korea and the Slovak Republic).
Remote consultations cannot be distinguished and are included in a few countries (such as Austria from 2020, and Ireland, Japan, Latvia, the Netherlands, the Slovak Republic and Spain from 2019).
In France, Germany, Luxembourg and Japan, more than three-quarters of spending was covered through a type of compulsory health insurance scheme.

This increase was particularly pronounced in Denmark, the United Kingdom, Austria and Japan, where the proportion of health spending attributed to preventive care was 7-8 percentage points above the share seen in 2013, reflecting substantial investments in public health measures related to fighting the spread of the COVID-19 pandemic.

With public health emergency measures phased out after the acute phase of the pandemic, the share of preventive spending dropped and reached pre-pandemic levels by 2023, ranging from 6-7% of total health spending in Canada and the United Kingdom to less than 3% in Poland, Belgium, Iceland, France, Switzerland, Portugal and Japan.
